Jacks or Better vs. Deuces Wild: Why the Same "Full Pay" Label Hides Different Odds

Published November 4, 2026 · 11 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

"Full pay" sounds like it should mean the same thing everywhere — the best version of a game, period. In video poker, it doesn't work that way. A full-pay Jacks or Better machine and a full-pay Deuces Wild machine are both, by definition, running the best commonly available pay table for their own game, and yet they land at noticeably different return percentages, require different strategy, and reward different kinds of hands entirely. Our pay tables guide already covers how a single payout swap can shift a game's return; this one compares two entire games that get lumped together constantly and explains why "full pay" on one tells you almost nothing about the other.

The mechanical difference: one wild card changes everything

Jacks or Better is draw poker with no wild cards at all — every hand you make, you make with the cards you're actually holding. Deuces Wild adds a single rule that reshapes the entire game: all four 2s act as wild cards, standing in for whatever card completes your best hand. That one change doesn't just make winning hands slightly easier; it rewires which hands are even worth building toward, because four cards in the deck now behave like universal substitutes rather than fixed values.

The downstream effect is a completely different hand-frequency profile. In Jacks or Better, a modest pair of jacks-or-better is your baseline winning hand and shows up constantly. In Deuces Wild, a pair alone doesn't pay anything at all — the baseline winning hand is bumped up to three of a kind, because wild deuces make three-of-a-kind-and-up dramatically more common than in a no-wild-card game, and the pay table is built around that shift.

The one-sentence version: Jacks or Better pays modestly and often; Deuces Wild pays nothing on small hands but compensates with bigger, more frequent wins further up the pay table, powered by the wild cards.

What "full pay" means in Jacks or Better

"Full pay" Jacks or Better almost always refers to the 9/6 pay table — 9 coins for a full house and 6 coins for a flush, per coin bet, with a royal flush paying the standard 4,000-coin jackpot at max coins. With perfect strategy, 9/6 Jacks or Better returns right around 99.5% to the player, which is why it's treated as the gold standard for the game and why serious video poker players actively hunt for it instead of assuming any Jacks or Better cabinet qualifies. Plenty of machines quietly run 8/5 or 6/5 pay tables instead, which look nearly identical on the glass but return meaningfully less.

What "full pay" means in Deuces Wild

Deuces Wild doesn't have a single universally agreed "full pay" label the way Jacks or Better does — there are several strong pay tables, and the one most commonly called full pay returns right around 100.76% with perfect strategy, meaning a mathematically perfect player is actually ahead of the house before any comps, promotions, or card-club points enter the picture. That number alone explains why Deuces Wild has such a strong reputation among advantage-minded players, and also why finding a genuinely full-pay Deuces Wild machine on a real casino floor is considerably harder than finding full-pay Jacks or Better — operators have less incentive to spread a table that mathematically favors a perfect player.

Look at how different the shape of these two tables is. Jacks or Better spreads its payouts across a wide range of modest hands, paying something on almost every pair you're dealt. Deuces Wild pays nothing until three of a kind, but makes up for it with a stack of extra top-end categories — four deuces, a wild royal, five of a kind — that simply don't exist in a non-wild game. Two games, two completely different payout shapes, both landing near the top of their respective category.

Why Deuces Wild needs a richer top end to hit the same return

A natural question is why Deuces Wild needs all those extra categories — four deuces, five of a kind, a wild royal — just to match or beat what Jacks or Better does with a simpler table. The answer is that wild cards make big hands so much more frequent that a pay table built like Jacks or Better's would return far more than 100% if it paid 9-and-6 on top of easy access to those bigger hands. The designers have to strip value from the small end (no pay on a pair, almost nothing on three of a kind) and concentrate it at the top, where wild-card-fueled hands are common enough to matter but still rare enough that a huge payout doesn't blow up the math. It's the same principle as our progressive jackpot guide describes for slots: a game's overall return has to balance somewhere, and a wild card is one of the biggest levers a designer has for shifting where that balance sits.

How strategy changes once deuces are wild

Because the baseline winning hand jumps from a pair to three of a kind, correct Deuces Wild strategy looks almost nothing like correct Jacks or Better strategy, even though both games are drawn from the same deck and the same five-card-draw structure. A hand you'd happily keep as a made pair in Jacks or Better — say, a pair of kings with three unrelated cards — isn't worth anything in Deuces Wild unless a deuce is involved, so a player who tries to apply Jacks or Better instincts to a Deuces Wild machine will consistently hold the wrong cards and give up a meaningful chunk of that game's generous return. Deuces Wild strategy instead revolves heavily around how many wild cards you're holding: zero deuces means you're playing something closer to a stripped-down version of regular draw poker strategy, while even a single deuce changes the entire decision tree, since a lone wild card alongside the right three natural cards can already be worth building toward four of a kind or better.

Which one actually suits you

Neither game is objectively "better" to play casually — they reward different temperaments. Jacks or Better pays out in small, frequent increments, so sessions feel smoother and your bankroll swings less violently, which suits a player who wants steady action over a long sitting. Deuces Wild's small hands pay nothing, so a session can run cold for stretches between the bigger wins that make up most of its return, which suits a player more comfortable with volatility in exchange for a game that, at full pay, is one of the few in the building that doesn't mathematically favor the house. Either way, the label "full pay" is only useful once you know which full-pay table you're actually comparing — a 9/6 Jacks or Better machine and a full-pay Deuces Wild machine sitting side by side on the same casino floor are both legitimately excellent versions of their own games, and neither one tells you anything about the other.

Frequently asked questions

Is Deuces Wild really better than Jacks or Better since its return is over 100%?

Only with perfect, computer-verified strategy and only on a genuinely full-pay machine — real-world play with small strategy errors gives up return quickly on both games, and short-pay Deuces Wild variants are common and return far less than the full-pay version.

Why doesn't a pair of aces pay anything in Deuces Wild?

Because wild deuces make three-of-a-kind-or-better hands common enough that the pay table has to start its payouts there instead of at a pair, or the game's overall return would run far higher than the designers intend.

Can I use Jacks or Better strategy charts for Deuces Wild?

No. The two games need entirely separate strategy charts because the value of nearly every starting hand changes once deuces are wild — a hand that's correct to hold in one game is frequently a mistake in the other.

Are there other common Deuces Wild pay tables besides the full-pay version?

Yes, several, and they're often labeled by their four-of-a-kind or straight-flush payout. Many of these short-pay versions look nearly identical to the full-pay table at a glance but return several points less, so it's worth checking the exact numbers rather than assuming any machine branded "Deuces Wild" is the strong version.

Which game has better variance for a small bankroll?

Jacks or Better generally suits a smaller bankroll better, since it pays something on a large share of hands and keeps losing streaks shorter, while Deuces Wild's higher overall return comes with longer stretches between paying hands.
